cemc-fryer-2003-01a.prompt: The marks of $32$ mathematics students on Test 1 are all multiples of $10$ and are shown on the bar graph. What was the average (mean) mark of the $32$ students in the class?

cemc-fryer-2003-01b.prompt: After his first $6$ tests, Paul has an average of $86$. What will his average be if he scores $100$ on his next test?

cemc-fryer-2003-01c.prompt: Later in the year, Mary realizes that she needs a mark of $100$ on the next test in order to achieve an average of $90$ for all her tests. However, if she gets a mark of $70$ on the next test, her average will be $87$. After she writes the next test, how many tests will she have written?

cemc-fryer-2003-02a.prompt:
In a game, Xavier and Yolanda take turns calling out whole numbers. The first number called must be a whole number between and including $1$ and $9$. Each number called after the first must be a whole number which is $1$ to $10$ greater than the previous number called.

The first time the game is played, the person who calls the number $15$ is the winner. Explain why Xavier has a winning strategy if he goes first and calls $4$.
cemc-fryer-2003-02a.answer: After Xavier calls $4$, Yolanda must call one of $5, 6, \dots, 14$; each of these is $1$ to $10$ less than $15$, so Xavier then calls $15$.

cemc-fryer-2003-02b.prompt:
In a game, Xavier and Yolanda take turns calling out whole numbers. The first number called must be a whole number between and including $1$ and $9$. Each number called after the first must be a whole number which is $1$ to $10$ greater than the previous number called.

The second time the game is played, the person who calls the number $50$ is the winner. If Xavier goes first, how does he guarantee that he will win?
cemc-fryer-2003-02b.answer: Xavier calls $6$, then always "completes 11": if Yolanda adds $n$, he adds $11-n$. He calls $6, 17, 28, 39, 50$.

cemc-fryer-2003-03a.prompt:
In the diagram, $ABCD$ is a square and the coordinates of $A$ and $D$ are $A(1, 4)$ and $D(1, 8)$, as shown.

The point $P$ has coordinates $(10, 0)$. Show that the area of triangle $PCB$ is $10$.
cemc-fryer-2003-03a.answer: $B(5,4)$, $C(5,8)$: base $BC = 4$, height = horizontal distance from $P$ to the line $x = 5$, which is $5$; area $\tfrac12(4)(5) = 10$.

cemc-fryer-2003-03b.prompt:
In the diagram, $ABCD$ is a square and the coordinates of $A$ and $D$ are $A(1, 4)$ and $D(1, 8)$, as shown.

Point $E(a, 0)$ is on the $x$-axis such that triangle $CBE$ lies entirely outside square $ABCD$. If the area of the triangle is equal to the area of the square, what is the value of $a$?

cemc-fryer-2003-03c.prompt:
In the diagram, $ABCD$ is a square and the coordinates of $A$ and $D$ are $A(1, 4)$ and $D(1, 8)$, as shown.

Show that there is no point $F$ on the $x$-axis for which the area of triangle $ABF$ is equal to the area of square $ABCD$.
cemc-fryer-2003-03c.answer: $AB$ lies on $y = 4$, so for any $F$ on the $x$-axis the height is $4$ and the area is $\tfrac12 (4)(4) = 8 \ne 16$.

cemc-fryer-2003-04a.prompt:
For the set of numbers $\{1, 10, 100\}$ we can obtain $7$ *distinct* numbers as totals of one or more elements of the set. These totals are $1$, $10$, $100$, $1+10=11$, $1+100=101$, $10+100=110$, and $1+10+100=111$. The "power-sum" of this set is the *sum* of these totals, in this case, $444$.

How many distinct numbers may be obtained as a sum of one or more different numbers from the set $\{1, 10, 100, 1000\}$? Calculate the power-sum for this set.

cemc-fryer-2003-04b.prompt:
For the set of numbers $\{1, 10, 100\}$ we can obtain $7$ *distinct* numbers as totals of one or more elements of the set. These totals are $1$, $10$, $100$, $1+10=11$, $1+100=101$, $10+100=110$, and $1+10+100=111$. The "power-sum" of this set is the *sum* of these totals, in this case, $444$.

Determine the power-sum of the set $\{1, 10, 100, 1000, 10\,000, 100\,000, 1\,000\,000\}$.
